title: Predictive Scheduling Laws by State and City (2027)
summary: Learn what predictive scheduling is, which states it impacts and how a single payroll and HR software can help your business comply.
body_markdown:
No employee wants to be surprised by abrupt shift changes. While emergencies can happen, frequent, last-minute rescheduling can make it difficult for people to manage their lives. Predictive scheduling laws in several states and cities seek to protect employees from abrupt shift changes by requiring businesses to provide schedules in advance.


While these laws help employees plan their lives effectively, they also pose compliance challenges for businesses. After all, scheduling enough talent to account for no-shows, sick days and bereavement can be tough, too. Certain industries have adopted on-call policies to offset these unexpected events, like in:


- [retail](https://www.paycom.com/who-we-help/retailers/)
- food service
- [hospitality](https://www.paycom.com/who-we-help/hospitality/)
- [manufacturing](https://www.paycom.com/who-we-help/manufacturing/)


Workers in these sectors are expected to be flexible. Predictive scheduling laws help ensure that flexibility stays *within reason* .


With so much predictive scheduling legislation emerging across the country, employers need to pay close attention to the laws in the states and cities where they operate. And we’ll help!


First, let’s examine how predictive scheduling laws work broadly and how they differ across jurisdictions. Then, we’ll explore how the right HR software simplifies predictive scheduling compliance.


## What are predictive scheduling laws?


Also known as “Fair Workweek” laws, predictive scheduling laws help workers avoid abrupt shift changes by requiring employers to provide schedules early. They also help prevent unexpected[“clopening” shifts](https://www.forbes.com/sites/retailwire/2014/08/19/starbucks-clopening-practices-deemed-inexcusable/?sh=1c2ba9e52250) — the practice of scheduling an employee to close and then open business the following day without sufficient rest.


Businesses that ignore these requirements could face fines and other penalties. At the same time, predictive scheduling laws often give employees the right to decline requests to change shifts. They can also help individuals establish reasonable expectations around flexibility and scheduling with their employers.


Some employees could fear retaliation when they push back on unreasonable requests — predictive scheduling laws help mitigate this concern. And while these rules are growing in popularity, they are *not* currently mandated at the federal level.


## What industries does predictive scheduling impact?


Predictive scheduling laws are most applicable to workplaces with hourly employees. Some of the most abrupt scheduling changes impact employees who earn minimum wage, but even supervisors could experience workplace whiplash if they can’t set their own schedule.


Consider these examples of employees who can be commonly affected by last-minute scheduling changes:


- a front-desk attendant at a busy, high-volume hotel
- a line cook for a 24/7 fast-food restaurant
- a warehouse auditor who counts inventory overnight
- a retail employee for a big-box store


## States with predictive scheduling laws


While certain states have passed predictive scheduling laws specific to certain cities, only one state has passed this kind of legislation statewide. However, it’s important to continue monitoring and understanding local predictive scheduling laws as they emerge because they could eventually influence broader, or state, guidance.


### *Oregon*


As of 2018,[Oregon](https://www.oregon.gov/boli/workers/pages/predictive-scheduling.aspx) is the only state with statewide predictive scheduling legislation. Oregon businesses with at least 500 employees in the retail, hospitality or food services industry must:


- provide workers with a “good faith” estimate of their schedule
- distribute written work schedules 14 days in advance
- grant a minimum of 10 hours of rest between shifts


Employees may still voluntarily accept back-to-back shifts within 10 hours, but employers must pay time and a half their normal rate (aka “predictability pay”).


As more predictive scheduling laws emerge, it’s important to consult your state government’s website for new bills and other updates.


## Cities with predictive scheduling laws


Predictive scheduling laws have gained the most traction in urban and densely populated areas. As of today, these eight cities — four in California alone — have enacted predictive scheduling laws:


### *1. Berkeley, California*


Since Jan. 12, 2024, Berkeley’s[Fair Workweek Ordinance](https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Fair%20Workweek%20Public%20Notice_City%20of%20Berkeley_January%202024%20%28English%29.pdf) requires businesses with 10 or more employees in the city to:


- post work schedules two weeks early
- provide 11 hours of rest between shifts
- offer additional hours to part-time employees before opening a new position


Importantly, this only applies to employers in certain industries — including health care, hospitality and food service — with global head count ranging from 56 to 100 or more employees.


### *2. Emeryville, California*


Introduced in 2018, Emeryville’s[Fair Workweek Ordinance](https://www.emeryville.org/Services/Business/Labor-Standards/Fair-Workweek-Ordinance) has given predictive scheduling guidance for retailers and fast-food restaurants with 56 or more employees globally and at least 20 working in Emeryville. The law requires employers to:


- provide a two-week notice for work schedules and 11 hours of rest between shifts
- compensate employees with one hour’s wage for any schedule changes made within 24 hours before a shift
- accept an employee’s right to decline a shift if the employee is given less than a two-week notice about an upcoming shift


### *3. Los Angeles, California*


Los Angeles enacted its[Fair Workweek Ordinance](https://wagesla.lacity.gov/fair-work-week-information) on April 1, 2023. The law covers retail businesses with 300 or more employees globally and requires those companies to:


- notify workers of their schedules 14 days in advance
- provide 10 hours of rest between shifts
- retain relevant documents — including work schedules — for at least three years


Consult the city’s[Frequently Asked Questions document](https://wagesla.lacity.org/sites/g/files/wph1941/files/2023-03/Fair%20Work%20Week%20FAQs.pdf) about the ordinance for more information.


### *4. San Francisco, California*


Enacted in its current form in 2016, San Francisco’s predictive scheduling law requires “formula retail establishments” with 20 or more employees to provide a two-week notice for work schedules and retain them — as well as payroll records — for at least *three years* .


A formula retail establishment (or “chain store”) is a business engaged in food or retail sales with at least 11 total locations. Use the city’s[affidavit for formula businesses](https://sfplanning.org/sites/default/files/forms/Formula_Retail_Affidavit.pdf) to determine if your business is covered.


### *5. San Jose, California*


In[San Jose](https://www.sanjoseca.gov/your-government/departments-offices/public-works/labor-compliance/opportunity-to-work#:~:text=The%20Opportunity%20to%20Work%20Ordinance%20took%20effect,to%20Work%20Notice**%20*%20**Hardship%20Exemption%20Application**) , the city’s predictive scheduling law requires employers with 36 or more employees to offer any extra work hours to preexisting, part-time employees before hiring new talent or contractors. However, this doesn’t mean employers need to offer additional hours if it would result in the part-time employee earning a premium rate, like overtime.


Additionally, employers in San Jose must provide a written notice of available hours *and* give their employees at least 48 hours to access those posted hours. (Though[fast hiring](https://www.sanjoseca.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/20083/636686520691730000) may be allowed in certain situations to serve peak demand.) This helps ensure preexisting employees have fair and reasonable access to consistent work schedules.


### *6. Chicago, Illinois*


Chicago’s[Fair Workweek Ordinance](https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/bacp/supp_info/fairworkweek.html) from 2020 (signed into law in 2019), as updated by revised rules effective June 1, 2026, requires certain employers with at least 100 employees worldwide to provide:


- two weeks’ notice for work schedules
- one hour of predictability pay for shift changes made less than 14 days in advance
- 10 hours of rest between each shift


Chicago also revised its Fair Workweek rules,[effective June 1, 2026](https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dol/rules-and-regulations-portal.html) , to clarify and expand scheduling obligations. The revisions:


- redefine “week” as any seven consecutive 24-hour periods
- require posted work schedules to be time- and date-stamped
- add detail to the required good-faith estimate, including on-call shifts


Notably, restaurants are unaffected by this law unless they have over 250 employees and 30 locations *total* . Additionally, employees are only covered by this law if their business meets the above criteria and they earn less than $64,945.55 in gross pay per year, up from $59,161.50 annually as of July 2025.


### *7. New York City, New York*


Signed in 2017, New York City’s[Fair Workweek Law](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dca/businesses/fairworkweek-deductions-laws-employers.page) requires fast-food employers to give workers:


- regular schedules that “stay the same” week to week
- a two-week notice for work schedules
- predictability pay for abrupt changes and “clopening” shifts
- just cause for reducing hours by more than 15%
- a chance to refuse extra work or clopening shifts


Separately, New York City’s Earned Safe and Sick Time Law was amended ([Int. 0780-2024](https://legistar.council.nyc.gov/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=6632607&GUID=97634BF6-0EAD-455B-8440-A50F25DABD61&Options=ID%7cText%7c&Search=780) ) to include the right to request temporary changes to an employee’s work schedule. This change took effect Feb. 22, 2026.


Additionally, affected companies must post the[NYC Fast Food Workers’ Rights poster](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/dca/downloads/pdf/workers/FastFood-FairWorkweek-Notice-English.pdf) in a visible area for employees.


### *8. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania*


Like Chicago’s ordinance, Philadelphia’s 2020 (passed in 2018)[Fair Workweek Employment Standards](https://www.phila.gov/media/20191218103134/Fair-Workweek-Law.pdf) primarily affect retail, hospitality and food service establishments with over 250 employees and 30 locations worldwide.


The law requires covered businesses to provide work schedules two weeks in advance and pay employees predictability pay for any changes made to the schedules within a 24-hour period of an affected shift.


### *9. Seattle, Washington*


One of the first predictive scheduling laws, the 2017[Seattle Secure Scheduling Ordinance](https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/LaborStandards/OLS_SS_one-pager_04-26-17.pdf) affects retail and food-service businesses with 500 or more employees worldwide. The law requires these employers to:


- engage in an “interactive process” with employees to establish a regular work schedule
- provide 10 hours of rest between shifts
- generate work schedules two weeks ahead of their effective date
- compensate employees with one hour of predictability pay for any hours added to their schedules with less than a two weeks’ notice


Since the specifics of these laws vary, always consult a licensed attorney to verify which predictive scheduling guidance affects the cities and states where your business operates.

## Which states don’t allow predictive scheduling?


As predictive scheduling laws gain traction elsewhere, 11 states prohibit their local governments from passing such legislation. Currently, predictive scheduling laws are banned in:


- Alabama
- Arkansas
- Florida
- Georgia
- Indiana
- Iowa
- Kansas
- Michigan
- Ohio
- Tennessee
- Wisconsin


## States considering predictive scheduling legislation


While some jurisdictions have enacted predictive scheduling laws and an even larger group has outright prohibited them, the concept remains up in the air for most of the nation. Even so, the following eight states have — at least in some form — considered enacting predictive scheduling:


- Connecticut
- Illinois
- Maine
- Michigan
- Minnesota
- New Jersey
- North Carolina
- Rhode Island


If your organization operates in any of these states, keep an eye out for more predictive scheduling legislation that could emerge. After all, even legislation that was shot down could speak to an uptick in similar proposals that may get passed.


## What are the penalties for noncompliance with predictive scheduling?


Given predictive scheduling laws are still relatively new in the areas they cover, not every jurisdiction enforces them. Those that do, however, may subject employers to costly, incremental penalties.


Keep the following penalties in mind if you operate in any of these cities:


- **Berkeley, CA** : Employers in Berkeley could receive a penalty of $1,000 for each affected employee and $500 for each provision of the law that was violated. Employers may also be expected to reimburse the affected employees $50 for each violated provision.
- **Emeryville, CA** : Employers in Emeryville could receive a penalty of $1,000 for each affected employee and $500 for each provision of the law that was violated.
- **Los Angeles, CA** : Employers in Los Angeles may be required to pay up to $500 to each affected employee for each provision of the law that was violated.
- **San Francisco, CA** : Employers in San Francisco may receive a penalty of $500 per legal violation.
- **San Jose, CA** : Employers in San Jose may receive a penalty of $50 for every employee and day in which they were noncompliant.
- **New York City, NY** : Employers that violate the Fair Workweek Law in New York City may receive a penalty of $500 for the first violation, $750 for a second violation *and* $1,000 for any subsequent violations within a two-year period.


## How does predictive scheduling impact employees?


At their core, predictive scheduling laws help avoid overworking or taking advantage of employees. One immediate benefit of this legislation is that it makes it easier for certain employees to plan their lives — potentially far in advance. In turn, this could improve a workforce’s:


- [well-being](https://www.paycom.com/resources/blog/workplace-mental-health/)
- engagement
- financial stability


The long-term benefit of these laws to employees will likely become clear as more predictive scheduling guidance emerges across the country.


## How does predictive scheduling benefit employers?


While predictive scheduling laws can be complex for businesses to manage, they can also help produce happier and more reliable employees. Though this may not be the only factor that influences their happiness, even small changes that improve an employee’s quality of life can yield benefits for their employer, too, such as:


- increased sales
- boosted productivity
- decreased turnover


Like with specific employee benefits, the positive impact of predictive scheduling laws on covered organizations should become clearer with time. Remember, this legislation is still relatively new and only enforced in a few jurisdictions.


## How to comply with predictive scheduling laws


Predictive scheduling laws often introduce a litany of requirements. But they are *not* impossible to maintain — especially with a truly[single HR software](https://www.paycom.com/resources/why-everyone-should-use-single-hr-software/) .

And the interface provides an instant, big-picture view of each worker’s availability. This way, leaders can easily identify any scheduling changes made within the last two weeks *or* see which employees haven’t received the required rest period between shifts.

## Predictive scheduling laws: FAQs


### *Who is covered by predictive scheduling laws?*


Currently, only certain employers in the specific, local jurisdictions where predictive scheduling laws exist are affected. Oregon, however, is the only state with statewide predictive scheduling guidance.


### *How do employers make shift and work hour changes under a predictive scheduling law?*


While the exact requirements vary across jurisdictions, most predictive scheduling laws require employers to notify their employees about a change to their shifts at least **two weeks** in advance. Some jurisdictions also let employees request temporary schedule changes. For example, New York City’s Earned Safe and Sick Time Act added this right on Feb. 22, 2026.


### *What are employers supposed to post to stay compliant with predictive scheduling laws?*


A confirmed schedule that is easily visible and accessible to all employees.


### *What are the key requirements of predictive scheduling laws?*


In general, predictive scheduling laws require employers to provide their employees with a confirmed schedule weeks in advance *or* pay their staff a premium for any abrupt changes. Ideally, this gives employees a chance to plan their lives and establish a reliable routine.


### *Are predictive scheduling laws the same across all states?*


No, predictive scheduling laws and the employers they affect often vary between jurisdictions — even within the same state. It’s important to verify the exact requirements of any predictive scheduling law that covers the area where your organization operates.


### ***Can predictive scheduling laws change across cities within the same state?***


Yes. Often, predictive scheduling laws are enforced at the local level, such as in California. However, a state could potentially pass a statewide law that may override city ordinances.


### *Are there any federal predictive scheduling laws?*


No, there is no federal requirement for predictive scheduling.


### *How far in advance do employers have to post schedules?*


If your organization is covered by a predictive scheduling law, at least two weeks’ notice is the general requirement to post shifts for employees. However, this requirement may vary based on the specific law that affects you.


### *Do employers have to notify employees before changing their schedules?*


If an employer is affected by a predictive scheduling law, yes, and the affected employee may be eligible for additional compensation depending on when they are notified. Employees may also have the right to request schedule changes. In New York City, for example, this right became part of the Earned Safe and Sick Time Act on Feb. 22, 2026.


### ***Which industries are required to follow predictive scheduling laws?***


Predictive scheduling laws generally affect employers in food service, hospitality, retail and warehouses. However, there is no general requirement for predictive scheduling laws to specify certain industries.
